title: Route on in-flight load, not request count
lesson: Round robin hands each replica the same number of requests, so when a 60k-token request and a 2k-token request cost very different amounts of work one replica saturates while another sits idle; counting the requests in flight on each replica and sending the next one to the lowest count (the SRE book's least-loaded round robin) keeps small requests from waiting behind heavy ones.
limitations: Illustrative scenario: the arrival order (heavy, heavy, small, small), the 6 s and 0.6 s service times, the 180 ms and 2.5 s response badges and the token sizes are an example. A token count is not a guaranteed proportional runtime, and round robin misroutes only when its rotation reaches a busy replica while another is free.

The in-flight count is a proxy for load, not a measure of work (the Google SRE chapter's own caveat): two replicas with equal counts can hold very different work. Least in-flight cannot tell them apart; the cut shows it helping only after short requests finish and the counts diverge. Weighted or utilisation-based policies, health checks, connection draining and long-lived connections are not shown; the baseline cut covers health checks.

The policy label changing on the balancer is a scene event. Routing policy is configuration enforced by the balancer or client library; a label, prompt or persistent instruction does not enforce routing, and by the same token persistent prompts do not enforce permissions.

The misrouted small request is drawn as waiting in a second slot until the heavy request completes. Real replicas may interleave work or queue in front of the process; the delay is the point, the exact mechanism is simplified.
Audio was measured and analysed (peak -1.0 dBFS, energy rise within 70 ms of each of 106 cues, spectrogram), not heard by a person.
transcript: 0:00.7–0:05.7 — Normal case under ROUND ROBIN. Three small '2k tokens' requests leave the client about a second apart. The balancer's pointer steps to Replica 1, 2 and 3 in turn; each replica's counter ticks to '1 in flight' and back to 0 as its slot finishes, and each response returns with a green '180 ms' badge.

0:07.3–0:12.0 — Costs diverge. A '60k tokens' request lands on Replica 1 and another on Replica 2; their slots fill slowly with a low ticking. A small request lands on Replica 3 and finishes at once. At 0:11.4 the three counters pop together: every replica has had exactly one request, yet they read 1, 1 and 0 because the short one is done.

0:12.2–0:16.7 — The misroute. The next small request leaves and the rotation points at Replica 1 anyway. It lands at 0:13.5 with a buzz and a jolt; Replica 1's counter turns orange at '2 in flight' and the request waits in a second slot. Replica 3's counter ripples green at 0:14.0 to show it was free. The heavy jobs finish and return grey envelopes; the delayed small response arrives last at 0:16.65 with an orange '2.5 s' badge.

0:18.0–0:19.3 — The fix. The balancer flashes green and its label changes in place to LEAST IN-FLIGHT; three green dots run from the counters up to the balancer's ports and a chime confirms the counters are now inputs.

0:19.8–0:26.8 — Resolution. Two heavy requests arrive while all counters are 0, so the tie falls back to rotation: Replica 2, then Replica 3. With the counters at 0, 1, 1 the next small request goes to Replica 1 (its counter flashes green at the pick) and returns in '180 ms' at 0:24.6; the one after that goes to Replica 1 again, where round robin would have sent it to busy Replica 2, and returns in '180 ms' at 0:26.75.
0:27.0–0:31.8 — The heavy jobs complete and all counters return to 0 under the LEAST IN-FLIGHT label; the stage holds, then fades to the title-only frame that also opens the video.
